source.title: Weak-to-Strong Elicitation via Mismatched Wrong Drafts

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or document mismatch.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly compares a weak-model-draft training intervention with no-draft GRPO and other draft variants, but uses RL with a verifier rather than fine-tuning on weak labels. It is a conceptual test of whether weak-model-derived information can elicit stronger-model performance, not a test of the original weak-label method or its PGR measure.
record.gate_note: The authors explicitly distinguish their method from supervised fine-tuning on weak labels: wrong drafts are injected into the stronger learner's GRPO context, with reward based on gold answers. Results below concern this intervention's math-task performance, not weak-to-strong supervised fine-tuning or PGR. The text also reports sampling pass@k curves, training dynamics, per-problem comparisons, and a reasoning-rigor scan; the rows focus on the endpoint accuracy results. Burns et al.'s findings are cited as prior work, not reported as this study's results.
record.test_reason: This study does not test weak-to-strong generalization in the claim's sense. The 'weak' Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B supplies wrong drafts that are placed in Mathstral-7B's GRPO prompt context. Reward comes from gold answers through a verifier. Nothing is trained on weak-model labels and no PGR is computed. The authors cite Burns et al. only to contrast their method: the weak model 'is not supervised-fine-tuning the strong learner.' The 'drafter' is also not clearly weaker on the task: it beats Mathstral base on AIME pass@1 (3.82 vs 0.81 on AIME 2025). The reader's 'tests/T2' contradicts its own finding that every version is not_tested; T6/discusses is the accurate relation.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is mostly right. Two additions are needed. First, the authors' headline framing is that this 'weak-to-strong elicitation' both sharpens and expands coverage under on-policy RLVR, which they present as a counterexample to the sharpen-only view of RL. Second, they identify the interaction of mismatch and wrongness as the active ingredient. They concede that AIME 2024 does not follow the pattern, that reward hacking is pervasive (96.7%), and that evidence comes from one model pair in one domain.
record.recipe_differences: Uses wrong drafts from Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, randomly mismatched to problems, as context during Dr. GRPO training of Mathstral-7B; uses an outcome verifier and gold answers for reward. It is not supervised fine-tuning on weak labels, and does not report PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcome varies by test set/year: mismatched-wrong is ahead on AIME 2025/2026, while no-draft GRPO leads it at pass@1024 on AIME 2024. Prompt format also changes reported endpoints; the text says the training-consistent format generally performs better.

fits_no_version.finding: Wrong drafts from Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, mismatched to the problem and placed in context during Dr. GRPO on Mathstral-7B, give higher MATH-500 greedy pass@1 than no-draft GRPO (71.98 vs 70.82, 10 seeds). On AIME 2025/2026 they also give higher pass@1024 (72.60/71.68 vs 66.94/61.58). On AIME 2024, no-draft GRPO leads at pass@1024 (72.97 vs 68.28).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Off-policy wrong drafts from a smaller model, mismatched to the training problem, can improve a larger learner's verifier-rewarded RL performance on some math benchmarks. The effect varies by test set.

record.problems: Evidence is limited to one learner, one draft model, and math tasks. AIME evaluation uses only 30 problems per year and two seeds; the paper notes possible contamination for AIME 2024 but says this is unverified. The outcome-only reward produces substantial reward hacking: a scan of 239 correct AIME rollouts judged 96.7% reward-hacked. Some reported comparisons use different prompt formats. PGR is not calculated.
record.rows_left_out: At the 60-row cap, omitted AIME 2024 pass@1 values for the selected and other configurations (Table 3), and other AIME 2024 pass@1024 configurations (Table 3). Also omitted per-difficulty MATH-500 values (Table 4), sampling pass@k curves (Figures 1, 3, 5), checkpoint trajectories (Appendix B, Table 6), per-problem AIME results (Figures 4, 6 and Appendix D, Tables 7–8), and reward-hacking scan outcomes (Appendix D, Tables 9–10). These are not PGR or weak-label fine-tuning results.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning on weak labels and no comparison against a strong ceiling trained on gold labels; PGR not computable. Gold-answer reward means the 'supervision' is not weak.
Draft-context variants are compared with no-draft GRPO, but none of these is a weak-label training change, and PGR is not measured.
Single learner/draft pair and a single math domain; no size, task or representation sweep in a weak-label setting.
AIME year differences and pervasive reward hacking (96.7% of 239 scanned correct rollouts) arise from the outcome verifier, not from exploiting a weak supervisor. No PGR under distribution shift.

record.verdict_notes: Row values check out against Tables 2–4 and Appendix B. In Table 4 only five overall values are listed because Matched+Correct collapses, so M3 (70.36) and M4 (69.02) are correctly taken from Appendix B. Appendix B reports mean±std, but the main text calls ±0.80 a 95% CI; this is a minor inconsistency in the paper. All rows correctly carry versions ['none']. The study title uses 'weak-to-strong', but the draft model outperforms the learner's base on AIME pass@1 and is described as 'more domain-trained'. It is therefore not a weak supervisor in Burns et al.'s sense.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on weak-model-produced labels; no PGR calculation for weak-label supervision.
The study compares GRPO draft-context variants, but does not measure PGR or compare the specified weak-label training changes against naive weak-label fine-tuning.
One learner, one draft model and one domain are used. The study does not calculate PGR or sweep model sizes or representations.

AIME years and reward-hacking behavior are examined, but the study does not measure PGR under distribution shift, student exploitation of what the weak supervisor cannot check, or the effect of shared student-supervisor errors.
No theoretical conditions for a student to beat its supervisor are tested.
No vision or other non-language modality is tested.
